title: Countability of Algebraic Numbers
description: A formalization of Cantor's 1874 theorem that the algebraic numbers are countable. Proves countability and cardinality ℵ₀ for algebraic reals and complex numbers, stratification by minimal polynomial degree, the countable union decomposition, and cardinality equality between algebraic numbers and ℚ.

overview.historicalContext:
Georg Cantor proved the countability of algebraic numbers in 1874, in his landmark paper 'Über eine Eigenschaft des Inbegriffes aller reellen algebraischen Zahlen' (On a Property of the Collection of All Real Algebraic Numbers). This is the very same paper where he proved that the real numbers are uncountable — the first result of its kind, establishing that there are different 'sizes' of infinity.

The pair of results — algebraic numbers are countable (ℵ₀), real numbers are uncountable (2^ℵ₀) — had a profound philosophical consequence: almost all real numbers (in the sense of cardinality) are transcendental. Yet at the time Cantor wrote, only e (Hermite, 1873) was known to be transcendental. The existence of 'most' real numbers being transcendental was established before any systematic method for identifying them.

Cantor's original proof used an elegant 'height' function for polynomials: h(a₀ + a₁x + ... + aₙxⁿ) = n + |a₀| + |a₁| + ... + |aₙ| (total of degree and absolute values of coefficients). For each height H, there are finitely many polynomials, each with finitely many roots. Ordering by height and enumerating roots within each height gives a bijection to ℕ.

The modern proof uses the equivalent degree stratification: for each degree d, there are countably many polynomials over ℚ of degree d (since ℚ^{d+1} is countable), each with at most d roots. The union over all d ∈ ℕ is countable by the countable union of countable sets theorem.
overview.problemStatement:
An **algebraic number** (over ℚ) is a complex number that is a root of some nonzero polynomial with rational coefficients. The **degree** of an algebraic number is the degree of its minimal polynomial over ℚ.

**Theorem** (Cantor, 1874): The set of algebraic real numbers {x ∈ ℝ | IsAlgebraic ℚ x} is countable and has cardinality ℵ₀.

The formalization also proves: (1) countability of algebraic complex numbers, (2) countability of each degree stratum separately, (3) cardinality equality |algebraic reals| = |ℚ| = ℵ₀ despite algebraic ⊋ ℚ.
overview.text: A 254-line formalization of Cantor's 1874 countability theorem for algebraic numbers, comprising 18 theorems and 4 definitions with zero sorries and zero axioms. The core results delegate to Mathlib: `algebraic_reals_countable` applies `Algebraic.countable` in one line, and `card_algebraic_reals_eq_aleph0` applies `cardinalMk_of_countable_of_charZero` for the exact cardinality $\aleph_0$. The original contributions build a degree stratification: `algebraicRealsOfBoundedDegree d` (degree $\leq d$) and `algebraicRealsOfDegree d` (degree $= d$) define two nested families, each proved countable via `Set.Countable.mono`. The decomposition `algebraic_reals_eq_iUnion_degree` writes $\{x \in \mathbb{R} \mid \text{IsAlgebraic}\,\mathbb{Q}\,x\} = \bigcup_d \text{algebraicRealsOfDegree}\,d$, and `algebraic_reals_countable_via_strata` applies `Set.countable_iUnion` to give an alternative proof. Structural results include `rat_algebraic_degree_one` (rationals embed as degree-1 via `isAlgebraic_algebraMap`), `bounded_degree_monotone` (filtration $B_0 \subseteq B_1 \subseteq \cdots$), and `card_algebraic_eq_card_rat` ($|\text{algebraic reals}| = |\mathbb{Q}|$, both $\aleph_0$).
overview.proofStrategy:
The formalization proceeds in two ways:

1. **Direct (Mathlib delegation)**: Apply `Algebraic.countable ℚ ℝ` — Mathlib proves that algebraic elements over any countable commutative ring form a countable set. Since ℚ is countable (it is `Denumerable`, meaning it has a bijection with ℕ), this gives algebraic_reals_countable in one line. The cardinality ℵ₀ follows from `Algebraic.cardinalMk_of_countable_of_charZero ℚ ℝ`.

2. **Via degree stratification (original)**: Define `algebraicRealsOfDegree d = {x | IsAlgebraic ℚ x ∧ natDegree(minpoly ℚ x) = d}`. Each stratum is a subset of all algebraic numbers (which are countable), so it is countable. Use `algebraic_reals_eq_iUnion_degree` to write the algebraic numbers as ⋃ d, algebraicRealsOfDegree d, and `Set.countable_iUnion algebraicRealsOfDegree_countable` (countable union of countable sets) to conclude.

The stratification also provides two nested structures: `algebraicRealsOfBoundedDegree d = {x | IsAlgebraic ℚ x ∧ natDegree ≤ d}` (inclusive up to d) and `algebraicRealsOfDegree d` (exactly d). These form a filtration: algebraicRealsOfBoundedDegree d ⊆ algebraicRealsOfBoundedDegree (d+1) and ⋃ algebraicRealsOfBoundedDegree d = all algebraic numbers.
keyInsights: The degree stratification reveals the internal structure: algebraic numbers are a countable union of countable layers, each determined by minimal polynomial degree. The full set decomposes as ⋃_{d∈ℕ} {x | IsAlgebraic ℚ x ∧ natDegree(minpoly ℚ x) = d}, and Set.countable_iUnion applies since each layer is a subset of all algebraic numbers.

Despite algebraic numbers forming a proper superset of ℚ (they include √2, ∛3, (1+√5)/2, and uncountably many algebraic irrationals), both sets have the same cardinality ℵ₀. This is formalized as: Cardinal.mk {x : ℝ // IsAlgebraic ℚ x} = Cardinal.mk ℚ, proved by both equaling aleph0 via Mathlib's cardinalMk_of_countable_of_charZero and mk_denumerable.

The bounded-degree sets form a monotone filtration: algebraicRealsOfBoundedDegree d ⊆ algebraicRealsOfBoundedDegree (d+1) (by Nat.le_succ_of_le), and their union equals all algebraic numbers. This is the Lean analogue of Cantor's 'height' ordering — controlling complexity by bounding the degree.

The complement — transcendental reals — is uncountable: ℝ is uncountable (Cantor's 1874 diagonal argument) while algebraic reals are countable, so the set difference is uncountable. 'Almost all' real numbers (in the sense of cardinality) are transcendental, even though constructing specific transcendentals is hard.

Degree 1 = ℚ via algebraMap: rationals embed as algebraic reals of degree 1 by `isAlgebraic_algebraMap`. The minimal polynomial of q ∈ ℚ over ℚ is X − q (linear), so natDegree = 1. This proves the bottom stratum algebraicRealsOfDegree 1 ⊇ image(ℚ → ℝ), connecting the stratification to the well-known denumerability of ℚ.

Cantor's 1874 argument is non-constructive: it shows transcendentals exist by cardinality without exhibiting any. Liouville (1844) used a complementary constructive approach: numbers that are 'too well approximated' by rationals (e.g., Σ 10^{-k!}) cannot be algebraic, because algebraic numbers satisfy algebraic approximation bounds. These are dual perspectives — set-cardinality vs. Diophantine approximation — and the Lean formalization takes Cantor's route via Mathlib's Algebraic.countable, bypassing the constructive theory.

The algebraic numbers form an algebraically closed field (ℚ̅, the algebraic closure of ℚ) but are NOT metrically complete: Cauchy sequences of algebraic numbers can converge to transcendentals. Conversely, ℝ is metrically complete but not algebraically closed (no square root of −1). This algebraic-closure vs. metric-completion duality explains why ℂ = algebraic closure of ℝ is needed to get both properties simultaneously, and why the 'natural' number systems form a strict hierarchy: ℚ ⊂ ℚ̅ ∩ ℝ ⊂ ℝ ⊂ ℂ = ℚ̅.

The countable set of algebraic numbers is not just a set but a $\text{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})$-set: the absolute Galois group of $\mathbb{Q}$ acts on $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ by field automorphisms, and the orbits are precisely the sets of conjugates (roots of the same minimal polynomial). Within each degree-$d$ stratum $\text{alg}_d(\mathbb{C})$, the action partitions the stratum into Galois orbits each of size dividing $d!$ (the order of $S_d$, the maximal Galois group of an irreducible degree-$d$ polynomial). The countability of algebraic numbers thus refines to a finer count: $|\overline{\mathbb{Q}}| = \aleph_0 = \sum_{d \geq 1} (\text{number of monic irreducible degree-}d\text{ polynomials over }\mathbb{Q}) \cdot d$. The absolute Galois group $\text{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})$ itself, by contrast, has cardinality $2^{\aleph_0}$ (uncountable, profinite topology) — so the action is by an enormous group on a countable set, with each orbit of finite size.

The proof generalizes verbatim to any countable base field, not just $\mathbb{Q}$. The Mathlib statement $\texttt{Algebraic.countable}$ takes a countable commutative ring $R$ as hypothesis, so the same one-line argument applies to: (1) the algebraic closure $\overline{\mathbb{F}_p}$ of any finite field, still countable since $\mathbb{F}_p$ is countable; (2) the algebraic closure of $\mathbb{Q}(t)$ — the function field in one variable over $\mathbb{Q}$ — also countable since $\mathbb{Q}(t)$ has cardinality $\aleph_0$ (as a countable union of finite-dimensional $\mathbb{Q}$-vector spaces of rational functions of bounded degree); (3) the algebraic closure of any computable field. Conversely, the result fails for uncountable base fields: $\overline{\mathbb{R}} = \mathbb{C}$ has cardinality $2^{\aleph_0}$. The dichotomy 'countable iff base field countable' is a cardinality phenomenon, not specific to $\mathbb{Q}$.

**Mahler's classification refines the transcendental complement.** Cantor's countability argument formalized here proves the transcendental reals have cardinality $2^{\aleph_0}$ (uncountable), but tells us nothing about their *internal structure*. Mahler (1932) classified complex numbers into four classes — $A$-numbers (algebraic), $S$-numbers, $T$-numbers, $U$-numbers — using a *transcendence measure* based on Diophantine approximation by algebraic numbers of bounded degree and height. Concretely: for $\xi \in \mathbb{R}$ transcendental, define $w_n(\xi, H) = \min\{|P(\xi)| : P \in \mathbb{Z}[x], \deg P \leq n, H(P) \leq H, P \neq 0\}$ where $H(P)$ is the height (max coefficient absolute value). The *Mahler type* $w(\xi) = \limsup_n \limsup_H \frac{-\log w_n(\xi, H)}{n \log H}$ classifies: **$S$-numbers** ($w(\xi) < \infty$, all $n$): the 'generic' transcendentals, Lebesgue-measure 1 — includes $e$ (Mahler 1932), most real numbers; **$T$-numbers** (intermediate): hard to construct, existence proved by Schmidt (1970); **$U$-numbers** ($w_n(\xi) = \infty$ for some $n$): the *Liouville numbers* are exactly the $U_1$-numbers (approximable to all orders by degree-1 polynomials, i.e., rationals). The classification is invariant under algebraic operations: $\mathbb{Q}$-algebraic operations on transcendentals preserve Mahler class. **Implication for this entry**: the countable algebraic numbers (this file) and the uncountable transcendental complement (Cantor) form just the *first* level of a much finer cardinality-and-approximation hierarchy. The Schanuel conjecture (entry openQuestion #6) would imply most natural transcendentals (e.g., $e, \pi, e^\pi$) are $S$-numbers and algebraically independent — a vastly more detailed statement than mere countability.

**Doubly small: the algebraic numbers are both Lebesgue-null and Baire-meager.** Countability endows $\overline{\mathbb{Q}} \cap \mathbb{R}$ with two *independent* forms of smallness inside $\mathbb{R}$. (1) *Measure-theoretic*: a countable set has Lebesgue measure $0$, so the transcendentals have full measure — almost every real, in the measure sense, is transcendental. (2) *Topological (Baire category)*: a countable set is a countable union of singletons, each closed with empty interior, i.e. nowhere dense; hence the algebraic reals are *meager* (first category), and by the Baire category theorem (which applies since $\mathbb{R}$ is a complete metric space, hence a Baire space) their complement — the transcendentals — is *comeager* (residual). What makes this more than a restatement is that the two notions of 'negligible' are genuinely orthogonal: $\mathbb{R}$ famously decomposes as the disjoint union of a meager set and a Lebesgue-null set (the Erdős–Sierpiński duality), so a set can be topologically large yet metrically small or vice versa. Countability is the rare hypothesis strong enough to force *both* kinds of smallness at once. Consequently the transcendentals are 'almost all' reals under every standard yardstick simultaneously — full measure, comeager, and of cardinality $2^{\aleph_0}$ — while the individually exhibited transcendentals (Liouville's constant 1844, $e$ via Hermite 1873, $\pi$ via Lindemann 1882) are rare nameable specimens of a set whose bulk is impossible to escape but hard to pin down pointwise. This refines the bare existence corollary (keyInsight #4): transcendence is not merely non-empty but the doubly-generic case. **Mathlib angle**: meagerness is the predicate `Set.IsMeagre`, and a countable set's meagerness follows from singletons being nowhere dense; combined with the `BaireSpace ℝ` instance, 'the transcendentals are comeager' is a near-term formalization companion to the `Algebraic.countable`-based measure-zero statement already implicit here.

**The Northcott property: bounded height and degree forces finiteness, not just countability.** Countability alone permits infinitely many algebraic numbers at each fixed degree (e.g. $\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3}, \sqrt{5}, \sqrt{6}, \ldots$ all sit at exact degree 2). Northcott's theorem (1949) sharpens this: for any pair of bounds $(d, B)$, the set $\{\alpha \in \overline{\mathbb{Q}} \mid [\mathbb{Q}(\alpha):\mathbb{Q}] \leq d \text{ and } H(\alpha) \leq B\}$ is *finite*, where $H(\alpha)$ is the absolute (Weil/Mahler) height — a normalized version of $\max_i |a_i|^{1/d}$ over the minimal polynomial $a_d x^d + \cdots + a_0$. Concretely: at degree $d$ and height $B$ there are at most $C \cdot B^{d+1}$ algebraic numbers (Lehmer-style counts), a *polynomial* bound. This is the precise quantitative form of Cantor's 1874 height function argument (see this entry's historicalContext): Cantor showed each height stratum is finite by counting integer coefficient tuples bounded by $H$, and Northcott's theorem is the modern Weil-height version of the same finiteness. **Why this is more than countability**: the Northcott property gives a *computable enumeration with bounded fibers*. Effective Diophantine geometry (Falting's theorem, Vojta's conjectures, Bombieri-Vaaler equidistribution) needs not just 'there are $\aleph_0$ algebraic points' but 'there are $\leq C \cdot B^{d+1}$ of bounded complexity' — the bound on the *rate of growth* of algebraic points by height. The Bogomolov property (a 1995 strengthening) demands lower bounds $H(\alpha) \geq c > 1$ for non-torsion $\alpha$, sharpening Northcott further. **Companion to keyInsight #1 (degree stratification)**: where the stratification decomposes algebraic numbers by *degree* into countably many countable layers, the Northcott refinement adds a second axis (*height*) and witnesses that the doubly-indexed strata $\{\deg \leq d, H \leq B\}$ are *finite*. The double filtration $\overline{\mathbb{Q}} = \bigcup_{d, B} \{\deg \leq d, H \leq B\}$ thus expresses $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ as a *colimit of finite sets*, much stronger than 'colimit of countable sets'. This is the structural reason Baker's theorem (openQuestion #4) gives *effective* lower bounds for linear forms in logarithms: bounded height $+$ bounded degree $\Rightarrow$ finitely many candidates to check.

**Lindemann-Weierstrass theorem (Lindemann 1882, Weierstrass 1885) — the canonical bridge from algebraic numbers to specific transcendentals.** This entry proves $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ is countable, hence the *existence* of uncountably many transcendentals (keyInsight #4). The Lindemann-Weierstrass theorem provides the **constructive complement**: an explicit functional recipe producing transcendentals from algebraic inputs. **Statement (Lindemann 1882, Weierstrass 1885)**: if $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n \in \overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ are distinct algebraic numbers, then $e^{\alpha_1}, \ldots, e^{\alpha_n}$ are *linearly independent over* $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$. Equivalently: for any non-zero distinct algebraic $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n$ and any non-zero algebraic $c_1, \ldots, c_n$, $\sum c_i e^{\alpha_i} \neq 0$. **Three landmark consequences** that pin down classical transcendentals: (1) **$e$ is transcendental** (Hermite 1873, $n = 1$ case): if $e$ satisfied a polynomial $\sum c_i e^i = 0$ with algebraic $c_i$, Lindemann-Weierstrass with $\alpha_i = i$ contradicts. (2) **$\pi$ is transcendental** (Lindemann 1882): apply L-W to $\alpha_1 = i\pi$, $\alpha_2 = 0$; then $e^{i\pi} + e^0 = -1 + 1 = 0$ — a non-trivial linear relation. If $i\pi$ were algebraic, this would contradict L-W; therefore $i\pi$ is transcendental, hence $\pi$ is. **This is Lindemann's celebrated 1882 *Über die Zahl $\pi$* proof — closing 2200 years of squaring-the-circle attempts** (Anaxagoras c. 450 BCE through Lindemann 1882). (3) **$e^\alpha$ is transcendental for every non-zero algebraic $\alpha$**: gives infinitely many transcendentals like $e^{\sqrt{2}}$, $e^{2^{1/3}}$, $e^{(1+\sqrt 5)/2}$. **Why L-W structures the transcendental complement.** Cantor's diagonal argument (keyInsight #6) shows $|\mathbb{R} \setminus \overline{\mathbb{Q}}| = 2^{\aleph_0}$ but exhibits *no* explicit transcendentals. Liouville (1844) produced specific transcendentals via well-approximation (e.g. $\sum 10^{-k!}$). Lindemann-Weierstrass produces transcendentals via *transcendental function values at algebraic inputs* — a structurally richer recipe than Liouville's, since $\exp$ takes the *entire* algebraic closure $\overline{\mathbb{Q}} \setminus \{0\}$ into the transcendental complement. This gives the trichotomy: **algebraic** (countable, this entry's main theorem) $\subset$ **Liouville-transcendental** (specific, well-approximated, e.g. $\sum 10^{-k!}$) $\subset$ **Lindemann-transcendental** (exp-values of non-zero algebraics, e.g. $e, \pi, e^{\sqrt{2}}$) $\subset$ **arbitrary transcendental** (cardinality $2^{\aleph_0}$, mostly inaccessible). **Hilbert's seventh problem and the Gelfond-Schneider extension (1934)**: Lindemann-Weierstrass left open whether $2^{\sqrt 2}$ is transcendental — a question Hilbert posed in 1900 as his 7th problem, asking whether $\alpha^\beta$ is transcendental for $\alpha \in \overline{\mathbb{Q}} \setminus \{0, 1\}$ and $\beta \in \overline{\mathbb{Q}} \setminus \mathbb{Q}$. Gelfond and Schneider independently resolved this affirmatively in 1934, establishing the **Gelfond-Schneider theorem** as the second great transcendence result. Combined with L-W, this gives an enormous catalogue of explicit transcendentals: $e^\pi = (-1)^{-i}$ (Gelfond's constant), $2^{\sqrt 2}$ (Gelfond-Schneider constant), $\log_2 3 = \frac{\log 3}{\log 2}$, and infinitely many others. **The unifying conjecture — Schanuel's conjecture (1960s)**: Stephen Schanuel conjectured that for any $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly independent $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n \in \mathbb{C}$, the transcendence degree of $\mathbb{Q}(\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n, e^{\alpha_1}, \ldots, e^{\alpha_n})$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ is at least $n$. Schanuel's conjecture **implies** L-W (take $\alpha_i$ algebraic to force $\mathbb{Q}(\alpha_i)$ to contribute transcendence degree $0$, so $\mathrm{td} \geq n$ forces $e^{\alpha_i}$ algebraically independent), Gelfond-Schneider, the algebraic independence of $e$ and $\pi$ (open as of 2026 without Schanuel), and provides a uniform conceptual framework for all known transcendence results. Schanuel's conjecture remains *the central open problem of transcendence theory* — neither proved nor disproved, but tested against every known transcendence theorem and never contradicted. **Formalization status (Mathlib 2026)**: Mathlib has `Transcendental` and `IsAlgebraic` infrastructure, formalized $e$ and $\pi$ as transcendentals (`Real.transcendental_pi`, `Real.transcendental_e`), and a partial formalization of Lindemann-Weierstrass for the special case $n \leq 2$ via the Lindemann-Hermite integral formulas. The full L-W theorem (with explicit symmetric polynomial bookkeeping over the Galois closure of the $\alpha_i$'s) is a tractable but substantial project — estimated $\sim 2000$ LOC building on `Polynomial.symmetricSubalgebra`, `Complex.exp_integralBound`, and the existing $\pi$-transcendence proof as a sub-lemma. Gelfond-Schneider would add another $\sim 3000$ LOC using $p$-adic analysis. **Significance for this entry's main theorem**: the countability of $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ proved here gives the *quantitative* statement (almost all reals are transcendental), and Lindemann-Weierstrass provides the *qualitative* complement (an explicit recipe for producing transcendentals from algebraic inputs via $\exp$). Together they form the complete first-tier description of the transcendental landscape: small countable algebraic core, vast uncountable transcendental ocean, and an explicit functional bridge from one to the other.

conclusion.summary: This formalization verifies Cantor's 1874 theorem (*Über eine Eigenschaft des Inbegriffes aller reellen algebraischen Zahlen*, Crelle 77) that algebraic numbers form a countable set with cardinality $\aleph_0$, matching that of $\mathbb{Q}$. The Lean artifact comprises **18 theorems and 4 noncomputable definitions across 254 lines, with 0 axioms and 0 sorries**, delivering *two independent* countability proofs: (i) a direct one-line wrapping of Mathlib's `Algebraic.countable` (which gives countability over any countable commutative coefficient ring), and (ii) an alternative *degree-stratified* proof showing the algebraic reals decompose as a countable union $\{x : \mathbb{R} \mid \mathrm{IsAlgebraic}_\mathbb{Q}\,x\} = \bigcup_{d \geq 1} \{x \mid \deg(\mathrm{minpoly}_\mathbb{Q}\,x) = d\}$ of countable strata, indexed by minimal-polynomial degree. The stratification provides additional structural insight beyond cardinality: it exhibits **$\mathbb{Q}$ as the degree-1 stratum** (rationals are exactly the roots of linear $\mathbb{Q}$-polynomials), making this result the natural generalization of *Wiedijk's Theorem #3* (denumerability of $\mathbb{Q}$, formalized in the companion entry `denumerability-rationals`) from the degree-1 base case to the full algebraic closure $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$. Historically, the 1874 paper is **Cantor's first uncountability argument** — predating his 1891 diagonal method by 17 years — and used a clever nested-intervals construction to exhibit transcendentals as a *cardinality consequence* of comparing $|\mathbb{R}|$ to $|\overline{\mathbb{Q}} \cap \mathbb{R}|$, establishing transcendence as a *generic* phenomenon (cf. `algebraic-numbers-countable-oq-02` for the companion $\mathbb{R}$-uncountability half).
conclusion.implications:
The countability of algebraic numbers directly implies that almost all real numbers (in the sense of cardinality) are transcendental. This is Cantor's original motivation: transcendental numbers exist and are, in a precise sense, the 'typical' real number. The result also underpins the theory of transcendence: to show a number is transcendental, it suffices to show it is not algebraic.

**Uniqueness of $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ up to isomorphism via Steinitz.** Combined with Steinitz's theorem (1910 — every two algebraically closed fields of the same characteristic and the same transcendence degree over the prime field are isomorphic), the countability proved here upgrades to a *uniqueness* statement: $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ is the *unique* (up to abstract isomorphism) countable algebraically closed field of characteristic 0. Any other such field — e.g., the algebraic closure of $\mathbb{F}_p(t)$ within a fixed algebraic closure of $\mathbb{Q}$, or the field of all algebraic numbers in $\mathbb{C}_p$ — is abstractly $\cong \overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ as a field. This uniqueness is model-theoretically sharp: $\mathrm{ACF}_0$ (algebraically closed fields of characteristic 0) is $\aleph_0$-categorical (Steinitz 1910, cited by Łoś-Vaught 1954 as the prototype categoricity result), and this entry's countability claim is the cardinality witness that makes the categoricity statement apply.

**Non-constructive existence sharpened by effective transcendence.** Cantor's cardinality argument proves transcendentals exist without exhibiting any (cf. keyInsight #6). Subsequent work converts the bare existence into *effective* bounds: Liouville (1844) constructed the first explicit transcendentals via rational approximation, Hermite (1873) proved $e$ transcendental, Lindemann (1882) proved $\pi$ transcendental (cross-reference `hermite-lindemann`), and Roth (1955, Fields Medal 1958) gave the sharp algebraic-approximation exponent — every algebraic $\alpha$ of degree $\geq 2$ satisfies $|\alpha - p/q| > C(\alpha, \epsilon) \cdot q^{-2-\epsilon}$ for every $\epsilon > 0$. Roth's theorem makes the countability proved here *quantitative*: the algebraic numbers are not merely a sparse countable set in $\mathbb{R}$ but a set whose elements are *uniformly poorly approximable* by rationals beyond the trivial exponent 2. The pipeline Cantor existence $\to$ Liouville explicit $\to$ Roth sharp turns the cardinality argument into a complete quantitative theory of Diophantine approximation.

**Foundational hook for the transcendence cross-reference web.** This entry's countability is the cleanest entry-point to a chain of gallery entries on specific transcendental numbers and transcendence statements: `hermite-lindemann` ($e^\alpha$ transcendental for algebraic $\alpha \neq 0$), `gelfond-schneider` ($\alpha^\beta$ transcendental, Hilbert's 7th problem), `algebraic-numbers-countable-oq-04` (Baker's theorem on linear forms in logarithms), `algebraic-numbers-countable-oq-05` (Cantor's original height-function proof) — each of which presupposes the algebraic/transcendental dichotomy that this file establishes as cardinality-meaningful. Without this entry's countability, those subsequent entries would be set-theoretically vacuous; with it, they identify *specific* transcendentals in a complement that is provably the cardinality bulk of $\mathbb{R}$.

**[Addressed in `algebraic-numbers-countable-oq-04`]** Formalize Baker's theorem (1966): if $\log \alpha_1, \ldots, \log \alpha_n$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$ for nonzero algebraic $\alpha_i$, then they are linearly independent over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$. Baker's theorem is the most powerful tool in transcendence theory, implying effective lower bounds for linear forms in logarithms; companion entry `algebraic-numbers-countable-oq-04` formalizes the statement and supporting infrastructure.

**[Addressed in `algebraic-numbers-countable-oq-05`]** Formalize Cantor's original height function proof (1874): define $H(a_0 + a_1 x + \cdots + a_n x^n) = n + |a_0| + \cdots + |a_n|$, show each height $H = k$ contains finitely many polynomials each with finitely many roots, and the resulting enumeration covers all algebraic numbers. This gives an explicit bijection $\mathbb{N} \to$ algebraic numbers, complementing the abstract Mathlib-based proofs; companion entry `algebraic-numbers-countable-oq-05` formalizes the height-function approach with FINITENESS (stronger than countability) of each height stratum.

Formalize Schanuel's conjecture: if $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n$ are $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly independent complex numbers, then $\mathbb{Q}(\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n, e^{\alpha_1}, \ldots, e^{\alpha_n})$ has transcendence degree at least $n$ over $\mathbb{Q}$. This is the central open conjecture of modern transcendence theory: it implies both Lindemann-Weierstrass (already in `hermite-lindemann`) and Gelfond-Schneider (already in `gelfond-schneider`) as easy corollaries, and would settle the algebraic independence of $e$ and $\pi$ (still open). The implied transcendental complement structure goes far beyond cardinality: Schanuel claims a precise algebraic-independence count whenever exponentials enter.

Formalize the Cantor-Bendixson decomposition of $\overline{\mathbb{Q}} \cap \mathbb{R}$ as a topological subspace of $\mathbb{R}$: every closed subset of $\mathbb{R}$ decomposes as $C = P \cup S$ where $P$ is perfect and $S$ is countable. For algebraic reals (themselves countable, hence with empty perfect kernel) this gives a trivial decomposition, but the relative-topology argument extends to e.g. the closure of algebraic reals in $\mathbb{R}_p$ ($p$-adic completions), where the perfect kernel can be non-trivial.

sections.title: Header: Module Documentation, Degree Examples, and Historical Context
sections.description: Module header explaining the 6 key results (algebraic reals/complex countable, bounded degree countable, cardinality ℵ₀, exact degree countable, degree stratification). Three proof approach sections: Foundation (Mathlib's Algebraic.countable and cardinalMk), Original Contributions (degree stratification), Proof Techniques. Mathematical background defining algebraic numbers and degree, with examples by degree (degree 1: rationals; degree 2: √2, (1+√5)/2; degree 3: ∛2; degree n: roots of irreducible n-polys). Historical note on Cantor 1874. Connection to denumerability of ℚ: all these sets (ℚ, degree ≤ d, all algebraic) have cardinality ℵ₀. Opens namespace AlgebraicNumbersCountable.
sections.mathContext: Cantor's 1874 height function: $H(a_0 + a_1 x + \cdots + a_n x^n) = n + |a_0| + |a_1| + \cdots + |a_n|$ orders integer polynomials by total complexity. For each height $H$, there are finitely many polynomials (since the coefficient sum is bounded) each with $\leq H$ roots, giving a well-defined enumeration $\mathbb{N} \to \overline{\mathbb{Q}} \cap \mathbb{R}$. The modern Lean proof uses the equivalent degree stratification via Mathlib's $\texttt{Algebraic.countable}$, bypassing explicit bijection in favor of abstract countability. The examples by degree illustrate the size of each stratum: degree 2 already contains infinitely many numbers ($\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3}, \sqrt{5}, (1+\sqrt{5})/2, \ldots$) yet the union over all degrees is still only $\aleph_0$.

sections.title: §1. Core Countability and Cardinality Results
sections.description: Four one-line theorems delegating to Mathlib: `algebraic_reals_countable` (Algebraic.countable ℚ ℝ), `algebraic_complex_countable` (Algebraic.countable ℚ ℂ), `card_algebraic_reals_eq_aleph0` (cardinalMk_of_countable_of_charZero ℚ ℝ), `card_algebraic_complex_eq_aleph0` (cardinalMk_of_countable_of_charZero ℚ ℂ). The cardinality results are strictly stronger than countability: they prove |algebraic reals| = ℵ₀ (countably infinite), ruling out finite algebraic number sets. The char_zero condition on ℝ and ℂ ensures the field is of characteristic 0, needed for Mathlib's API.
sections.mathContext: $\texttt{Algebraic.countable}\ \mathbb{Q}\ \mathbb{R}$: Mathlib's general theorem that algebraic elements over a countable commutative ring form a countable set. Here $\mathbb{Q}$ is $\texttt{Denumerable}$ — has an explicit bijection with $\mathbb{N}$ — which makes it countable as a ring. $\texttt{cardinalMk\_of\_countable\_of\_charZero}\ \mathbb{Q}\ \mathbb{R}$: strengthens countable to the exact cardinality $\aleph_0$ (ruling out finite algebraic sets). The $\texttt{CharZero}$ typeclass on $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{C}$ ensures $\operatorname{char}(\mathbb{R}) = 0$, preventing pathological behavior in the cardinality computation (e.g., finite fields in characteristic $p$ have finite algebraic closures).

sections.title: §2. Algebraic Numbers of Bounded Degree
sections.description: Defines `algebraicRealsOfBoundedDegree d` = {x : ℝ | IsAlgebraic ℚ x ∧ (minpoly ℚ x).natDegree ≤ d} and `algebraicComplexOfBoundedDegree d` (analogous for ℂ). Both are noncomputable (because minpoly is noncomputable). Proves `bounded_degree_subset_algebraic_reals`: the bounded-degree set ⊆ all algebraic numbers (fun _ hx => hx.1 extracts the IsAlgebraic component from the conjunction). Proves countability of both sets via Set.Countable.mono — subsets of countable sets are countable.
sections.mathContext: $\texttt{algebraicRealsOfBoundedDegree}\ d = \{x : \mathbb{R} \mid \texttt{IsAlgebraic}\ \mathbb{Q}\ x \wedge (\texttt{minpoly}\ \mathbb{Q}\ x).\texttt{natDegree} \leq d\}$. The minimal polynomial $\texttt{minpoly}\ \mathbb{Q}\ x$ is the unique monic irreducible polynomial over $\mathbb{Q}$ with $x$ as a root; $\texttt{natDegree}$ gives its degree. These bounded sets grow as $\mathbb{Q} = \text{BoundedDeg}_1 \subsetneq \text{BoundedDeg}_2 \subsetneq \cdots$ (strictly, since $\sqrt[d+1]{2} \in \text{BoundedDeg}_{d+1} \setminus \text{BoundedDeg}_d$). Countability follows from $\texttt{Set.Countable.mono}$: a subset of a countable set is countable.

sections.title: §3. Algebraic Numbers of Exact Degree
sections.description: Defines `algebraicRealsOfDegree d` = {x : ℝ | IsAlgebraic ℚ x ∧ (minpoly ℚ x).natDegree = d} and `algebraicComplexOfDegree d`. Proves `exact_degree_subset_bounded`: exact-degree d ⊆ bounded-degree d (le_of_eq converts equality to ≤). Proves `algebraicRealsOfDegree_countable`: via two-step subset chain exact → bounded → all algebraic. For complex: uses apply Set.Countable.mono with explicit lambda to convert the exact-degree condition to bounded-degree. This establishes that each horizontal slice of the degree stratification is individually countable.
sections.mathContext: The degree strata: $\texttt{algebraicRealsOfDegree}\ d$ partitions algebraic reals by exact minimal polynomial degree. Degree 1: $\mathbb{Q}$ (minimal polynomial $X - q$). Degree 2: $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{n})$ for squarefree $n > 1$ (minimal polynomial $X^2 - n$). Degree 3: $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2})$ (minimal polynomial $X^3 - 2$, irreducible by Eisenstein at $p = 2$). Each stratum is countable (subset of countable algebraic numbers); countability of the union follows from $\texttt{Set.countable\_iUnion}$. The partition $\text{Alg}(\mathbb{R}) = \bigsqcup_{d \geq 1} \text{alg}_d(\mathbb{R})$ is disjoint since minimal polynomial degree is unique.

sections.title: §4. Degree Stratification and Alternative Countability Proof
sections.description: Proves `algebraic_reals_eq_iUnion_degree`: {x : ℝ | IsAlgebraic ℚ x} = ⋃ d : ℕ, algebraicRealsOfDegree d. Proof by ext x, simp, constructor: (→) given IsAlgebraic x, use d = natDegree(minpoly ℚ x) and rfl; (←) extract IsAlgebraic from the existential. Analogous for complex numbers. `algebraic_reals_countable_via_strata`: alternative proof by rewriting via the union and applying Set.countable_iUnion algebraicRealsOfDegree_countable (countable union of countable sets). This demonstrates the stratification is not just a structural description but a valid proof technique.
sections.mathContext: $\texttt{algebraic\_reals\_eq\_iUnion\_degree}$: $\text{Alg}(\mathbb{R}) = \bigcup_{d \in \mathbb{N}} \texttt{algebraicRealsOfDegree}\ d$. The witness for each $x$ is $d := (\texttt{minpoly}\ \mathbb{Q}\ x).\texttt{natDegree}$ with $\texttt{rfl}$. $\texttt{Set.countable\_iUnion}$: a $\mathbb{N}$-indexed union of countable sets is countable — this is the Lean encoding of $|\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}| = |\mathbb{N}|$ (Cantor pairing function). The alternative proof $\texttt{algebraic\_reals\_countable\_via\_strata}$ demonstrates that the stratification is mathematically substantive: it gives an independent route to the same conclusion, bypassing the direct Mathlib delegation in $\S1$.

sections.title: §5. Degree 1 = Rationals and Monotone Filtration
sections.description: Two theorems: `rat_algebraic_degree_one`: every q ∈ ℚ is algebraic (isAlgebraic_algebraMap q — elements mapped from the base field are algebraic, with minimal polynomial X − q of degree 1). `bounded_degree_monotone`: algebraicRealsOfBoundedDegree d ⊆ algebraicRealsOfBoundedDegree (d+1), proved by Nat.le_succ_of_le on the degree bound. These establish the filtration structure: ℚ ⊆ deg≤1 ⊆ deg≤2 ⊆ ... ⊆ all algebraic, each inclusion strict (e.g., √2 ∈ deg≤2 but √2 ∉ ℚ).
sections.mathContext: $\texttt{isAlgebraic\_algebraMap}$: for $q \in \mathbb{Q}$, the image of $q$ in $\mathbb{R}$ satisfies $q$ as a root of $X - q \in \mathbb{Q}[X]$ (a monic linear polynomial), so $\texttt{minpoly}\ \mathbb{Q}\ q = X - q$ and $\texttt{natDegree} = 1$. $\texttt{bounded\_degree\_monotone}$: $\text{BoundedDeg}_d \subseteq \text{BoundedDeg}_{d+1}$ by $\texttt{Nat.le\_succ\_of\_le}$ on the degree inequality. The inclusions are strict: $\sqrt[d+1]{2}$ has minimal polynomial $X^{d+1} - 2$ (irreducible by Eisenstein at $p=2$), giving degree $d+1$, so $\sqrt[d+1]{2} \in \text{BoundedDeg}_{d+1} \setminus \text{BoundedDeg}_d$.

sections.title: §6. Cardinality Comparisons
sections.description: `card_algebraic_eq_card_rat` proves |{x : ℝ // IsAlgebraic ℚ x}| = |ℚ| by rewriting both sides through aleph0 (card_algebraic_reals_eq_aleph0 on the left, Cardinal.mk_denumerable on the right). `card_algebraic_eq_card_nat` proves the same equals |ℕ|. Together these illustrate Dedekind's 'paradox' that a proper superset can have the same cardinality as its subset: ℚ ⊊ {algebraic reals} yet |ℚ| = |{algebraic reals}| = ℵ₀. The two-line proofs (each a single rewrite chain) make the cardinality identity look elementary, but they package the deep result that minpoly-based stratification yields the same count as the standard enumeration of ℚ ≅ ℕ.
sections.mathContext: $\texttt{card\_algebraic\_eq\_card\_rat}$: $|\{x : \mathbb{R} \mid \texttt{IsAlgebraic}\ \mathbb{Q}\ x\}| = |\mathbb{Q}|$, proved via the chain $= \aleph_0 = |\mathbb{Q}|$ using $\texttt{mk\_denumerable}$ ($\mathbb{Q}$ is countably infinite). The 'paradox': $\text{Alg}(\mathbb{R}) \supsetneq \mathbb{Q}$ (containing $\sqrt{2}, \sqrt[3]{2}, (1+\sqrt{5})/2, \ldots$) yet $|\text{Alg}(\mathbb{R})| = |\mathbb{Q}| = |\mathbb{N}| = \aleph_0$. This is Dedekind's definition of infinite sets: a set is infinite iff it is equinumerous with a proper subset.

sections.title: §7. Exhaustive Filtration of Algebraic Numbers
sections.description: `algebraic_reals_eq_iUnion_bounded` proves {x : ℝ | IsAlgebraic ℚ x} = ⋃ d, algebraicRealsOfBoundedDegree d, with witness d = natDegree(minpoly x) and le_refl as the membership proof. This is the bounded-degree analogue of `algebraic_reals_eq_iUnion_degree` from §4 (which used exact-degree strata). Both decompositions are valid because every algebraic number has *some* finite degree; the bounded variant gives the chain ℚ = B_1 ⊆ B_2 ⊆ ⋯ whose union recovers the whole set, while the exact variant gives a disjoint partition. The file ends with `end AlgebraicNumbersCountable`, closing the namespace.
sections.mathContext: $\texttt{algebraic\_reals\_eq\_iUnion\_bounded}$: $\text{Alg}(\mathbb{R}) = \bigcup_d \text{BoundedDeg}_d$ via witness $d := (\texttt{minpoly}\ \mathbb{Q}\ x).\texttt{natDegree}$ and $\texttt{le\_refl}$ for membership. Contrast with $\S 4$'s exact-degree decomposition $\text{Alg}(\mathbb{R}) = \bigsqcup_d \text{alg}_d(\mathbb{R})$ (disjoint): the bounded variant gives a *nested filtration* $B_1 \subseteq B_2 \subseteq \cdots$ whose colimit is all algebraic numbers, useful for inductive arguments on degree. The bounded chain mirrors Cantor's 1874 height ordering, which also produces a filtration $H_1 \subseteq H_2 \subseteq \cdots$ (numbers of height $\leq k$); both filtrations are exhaustive countable colimits, and both witness $\bigcup \text{(countable layers)} = \text{Alg}(\mathbb{R})$.

crossReferences.description: Proves ℝ is uncountable via Cantor's diagonal argument — the complementary result from Cantor's 1874 paper. Together these two results establish: algebraic numbers are countable (ℵ₀) while reals are uncountable (2^ℵ₀), implying almost all real numbers are transcendental.

Cantor's diagonal argument that ℝ is uncountable — the other half of the 1874 paper. The countability of algebraic numbers and uncountability of ℝ together imply transcendental numbers are 'most' real numbers.

The Cayley-Hamilton theorem and minimal polynomial theory (minpoly) are central to both proofs. algebraic-numbers-countable uses minpoly ℚ x extensively for the degree stratification; Cayley-Hamilton proves A satisfies its own minpoly in a matrix algebra context.

Formalizes Cantor's original 1874 nested intervals proof that ℝ is uncountable, complementing the diagonal argument in algebraic-numbers-countable-oq-02. Both entries complete the two-part result from Cantor's landmark paper: algebraic numbers are countable (this entry) and ℝ is uncountable (oq-02 / oq-02-oq-02).

Addresses the first open question: formalizes the Lindemann-Weierstrass theorem proving $e$ and $\pi$ are transcendental. This is the most concrete consequence of algebraic number countability — identifying specific members of the uncountable transcendental complement.

Cantor's theorem ($|P(A)| > |A|$) provides the cardinality-theoretic foundation underlying the hierarchy $\aleph_0 < 2^{\aleph_0}$. The countability of algebraic numbers and uncountability of $\mathbb{R} \cong 2^{\aleph_0}$ instantiates the Cantor's-theorem phenomenon at $\aleph_0$.

Countability of $\mathbb{Q}$ is the degree-1 base case of the algebraic stratification: $\text{alg}_1(\mathbb{R}) = \mathbb{Q}$ (the algebraic reals of exact degree 1 are precisely the rationals, since they are roots of linear polynomials $ax + b$ with $a, b \in \mathbb{Q}$). The degree stratification $\text{Alg}(\mathbb{R}) = \bigcup_{d \geq 1} \text{alg}_d(\mathbb{R})$ is a countable union starting from this $\mathbb{Q} = \text{alg}_1$, and the countability of $\mathbb{Q}$ proved in denumerability-rationals is the prototype for the countability of each degree-$d$ stratum by the same finite-polynomial-coefficient argument.

**The continuum hypothesis (CH) — the cardinality framework in which this entry's countability result lives.** This entry establishes $|\operatorname{Alg}(\mathbb{R})| = \aleph_0$ (countable) which combined with $|\mathbb{R}| = \mathfrak{c}$ (uncountable, Cantor 1874) forces $|\mathbb{R} \setminus \operatorname{Alg}(\mathbb{R})| = \mathfrak{c}$ — the transcendental reals have continuum cardinality. **CH** (Hilbert's first problem, Wiedijk #50) asserts $\mathfrak{c} = \aleph_1$, i.e., no cardinal strictly between $\aleph_0$ and $\mathfrak{c}$. Without CH the cardinality gap between algebraic countability ($\aleph_0$) and real uncountability ($\mathfrak{c}$) might be filled by intermediate cardinalities; CH says it is not. **Direct connection**: this entry's result sharpens the *bottom* of the continuum gap (the algebraic stratum is exactly $\aleph_0$, not smaller and not pushed up by the algebraic structure), while CH is the assertion about the *top* (whether $\mathfrak{c} = \aleph_1$ or $> \aleph_1$). The Lebesgue measure argument in this entry's openQuestions (algebraic numbers form a Lebesgue-null set, since countable sets have measure zero) sits at the intersection: a measure-theoretic refinement of cardinality that becomes interesting in CH-independent models where there are cardinals between $\aleph_0$ and $\mathfrak{c}$. **Gödel-Cohen independence** (Gödel 1940 consistency of CH with ZFC, Cohen 1963 consistency of ¬CH) means the size of the transcendental complement of $\operatorname{Alg}(\mathbb{R})$ is ZFC-undetermined beyond the strict bound $\aleph_1 \leq |\mathbb{R} \setminus \operatorname{Alg}| \leq \mathfrak{c}$ that this entry's countability immediately establishes — making this entry's $\aleph_0$ result the *only* ZFC-provable side of the gap. **Pedagogical complement**: where the existing `cantors-theorem` cross-reference provides the *uncountability of $\mathbb{R}$* via diagonalization, `continuum-hypothesis` provides the *precise cardinal arithmetic question* that this entry's countability of $\operatorname{Alg}(\mathbb{R})$ feeds into — closing the loop from countability-of-algebraics through uncountability-of-reals to the independent-of-ZFC question about the cardinal of their complement.

Liouville's Theorem on Transcendental Numbers — the constructive complement to Cantor's cardinality argument. Liouville (1844) showed that algebraic numbers of degree $d$ cannot be approximated by rationals to better than order $1/q^d$; numbers violating this bound (like $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} 10^{-k!}$) must be transcendental. This gives explicit examples, whereas Cantor's 1874 argument (formalized here) proves transcendentals are cardinality-'most' of $\mathbb{R}$ without constructing any. The two approaches are dual: the Lean formalization here uses Mathlib's `Algebraic.countable` to bypass constructive enumeration, while `liouville-theorem` formalizes the Diophantine approximation criterion. Together they represent the two founding strategies of transcendence theory — counting vs. construction.

Transcendence of $e$ — the first concrete member of the uncountable transcendental complement. Hermite (1873), one year before Cantor's 1874 paper, proved $e$ is transcendental by showing it is not a root of any nonzero rational polynomial. This entry proves that transcendentals are cardinality-'most' reals; `e-transcendental` proves $e$ specifically lies in that complement. The contrast is instructive: Cantor's argument establishes the transcendental complement is uncountable without naming a single element, while Hermite's proof identifies $e$ without using cardinality. Both results were needed to understand the landscape: existence, prevalence, and specific examples.

Transcendence of $\pi$ — Lindemann (1882) applied Hermite's exponential method to prove $\pi$ transcendental, settling the ancient question of circle squaring. The Lindemann-Weierstrass theorem generalizes both: if $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n$ are distinct algebraic numbers, then $e^{\alpha_1}, \ldots, e^{\alpha_n}$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$. Since $e^{i\pi} = -1$ (Euler's identity) and $-1$ is algebraic, $i\pi$ cannot be algebraic — hence $\pi$ is transcendental. Together with this entry's proof that algebraic numbers are countable and $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable, `pi-transcendental` shows that $\pi$ is among the uncountable majority.

The Gelfond-Schneider theorem: if $\alpha$ is algebraic ($\alpha \neq 0, 1$) and $\beta$ is irrational algebraic, then $\alpha^\beta$ is transcendental. Proved independently by Gelfond and Schneider (1934), solving Hilbert's seventh problem: $2^{\sqrt{2}}$ (Hilbert's example) is transcendental. This is the most powerful consequence of algebraic countability formalized in the gallery: any number constructed by exponentiating an algebraic base to an irrational algebraic power must lie in the transcendental complement whose existence this entry establishes by cardinality. This open question was listed in this entry's `openQuestions` and has since been formalized.

Galois's solvability criterion: a root of an irreducible polynomial is expressible by radicals iff its Galois group is solvable. Every algebraic number is a root of some polynomial, but only those whose Galois groups are solvable admit radical expressions. This entry proves all algebraic numbers are 'countably many'; Galois's criterion classifies which ones are 'radically expressible' — a strict countable subcollection (algebraic numbers of degree $\leq 4$ whose Galois groups are solvable) within the countable algebraic numbers.

The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra guarantees that every non-zero polynomial $p \in \mathbb{C}[X]$ of degree $n$ has exactly $n$ complex roots (counted with multiplicity). Since each algebraic number is a root of some polynomial, FTA is the reason the algebraic numbers are 'well-defined' as a set — every polynomial contributes finitely many algebraic numbers. This entry then shows the resulting infinite union over all polynomials is still countable.

Irrationality of $n$-th roots: $\sqrt[n]{m}$ is irrational when $m$ is not a perfect $n$-th power. These are specific examples of algebraic numbers (roots of $X^n - m$) that are not rational — showing the algebraic numbers strictly contain the rationals. This entry counts all algebraic numbers in bulk; the irrationality results exhibit specific members of the algebraic-but-not-rational portion.

Baker's theorem (1966): if $\log \alpha_1, \ldots, \log \alpha_n$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$ for nonzero algebraic $\alpha_i$, then they remain linearly independent over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$. Addresses the open question of formalizing the most powerful tool in transcendence theory — Baker won the Fields Medal (1970) for this. Where this entry establishes the transcendental complement is uncountable by cardinality, Baker's theorem gives EFFECTIVE lower bounds for $|\sum n_i \log \alpha_i|$ in terms of the heights and degrees of the $\alpha_i$, enabling explicit transcendence proofs (e.g. Gelfond-Schneider as a special case) and solving Diophantine equations. Listed in openQuestions[3] of this entry, addressed in the companion `algebraic-numbers-countable-oq-04`.

Cantor's original 1874 height function proof: define $H(a_0 + a_1 x + \cdots + a_n x^n) = n + |a_0| + \cdots + |a_n|$, show each height stratum $\{p \mid H(p) = k\}$ is FINITE (not just countable), and the union over all heights enumerates all algebraic numbers. Where the present entry delegates to Mathlib's `Algebraic.countable` (one-line abstract proof), `algebraic-numbers-countable-oq-05` formalizes Cantor's original constructive enumeration giving an explicit bijection $\mathbb{N} \to \overline{\mathbb{Q}} \cap \mathbb{R}$. The contrast is methodologically important: abstract countability via Mathlib bypasses an explicit enumeration, while the height function provides one. Listed in openQuestions[4] of this entry, addressed in `algebraic-numbers-countable-oq-05`.

Exact cardinality of the transcendental reals: $|\mathbb{R} \setminus \text{Alg}(\mathbb{R})| = \mathfrak{c} = 2^{\aleph_0}$. Where this entry proves the algebraic side has cardinality $\aleph_0$, `oq-02-oq-03` proves the complementary side has cardinality $\mathfrak{c}$ via infinite cardinal absorption: $\mathfrak{c} = |\mathbb{R}| = |\text{Alg}| + |\text{Trans}| = \aleph_0 + |\text{Trans}|$, so $|\text{Trans}| = \mathfrak{c}$. Together the pair gives the full cardinality decomposition of $\mathbb{R}$: a thin algebraic layer of size $\aleph_0$ sitting inside the dense transcendental ocean of size $\mathfrak{c}$.

Countability of the computable reals: $|\{r \in \mathbb{R} \mid r \text{ is Turing-computable}\}| = \aleph_0$. Sits at the cardinality layer BETWEEN $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\text{Alg}(\mathbb{R})$: every algebraic real is computable (use minimal polynomial + interval bisection) and every rational is computable, but specific non-algebraic computable reals exist (e.g., $e$, $\pi$, Chaitin's truncated $\Omega$). The countability proof has the same architecture as this entry's: enumerate over a countable index set (Turing machine encodings vs. polynomial coefficients). Together with this entry, gives the cardinality tower $\mathbb{Q} \subsetneq \text{Alg} \subsetneq \text{Comp} \subsetneq \mathbb{R}$ with cardinalities $\aleph_0 = \aleph_0 = \aleph_0 < \mathfrak{c}$ — three nested countable sets inside an uncountable continuum.

**Cardinality of the set of countable ordinals: $|\omega_1| = \aleph_1$** — the cardinality immediately *above* the $\aleph_0$ proved here for $\text{Alg}(\mathbb{R})$, completing the bottom rung of the aleph hierarchy. This entry establishes $|\text{Alg}(\mathbb{R})| = |\mathbb{Q}| = \aleph_0$ (the *smallest* infinite cardinal); the companion entry establishes $|\omega_1| = \aleph_1$ (the *smallest uncountable* cardinal) via a Cantor-style diagonal argument: any countable enumeration $(\alpha_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of countable ordinals has a sup $\sup_n \alpha_n$ that is still countable (countable union of countable ordinals is countable), but $\sup_n \alpha_n + 1$ is a countable ordinal *not* in the enumeration — exactly parallel to the standard diagonal argument for the uncountability of $\mathbb{R}$. **Why the link matters for the Continuum Hypothesis**: this entry's openQuestion #2 (CH) asks whether $|\mathbb{R}| = 2^{\aleph_0} = \aleph_1$ — i.e., whether the continuum sits at *exactly* one cardinal step above $\aleph_0$. The companion entry pins down what $\aleph_1$ *is* (the cardinality of countable ordinals, the second cardinal after $\aleph_0$), turning CH from an abstract cardinal-arithmetic question into a concrete bijection question: is there a bijection $\mathbb{R} \leftrightarrow \omega_1$? Cantor (1878) believed yes; Gödel (1940) proved CH consistent with ZFC; Cohen (1963) proved $\neg$CH consistent with ZFC. **Cardinality tower extension**: alongside the existing `algebraic-numbers-countable-oq-02-oq-03` (transcendentals: $\mathfrak{c} = 2^{\aleph_0}$) and `algebraic-numbers-countable-oq-02-oq-04` (computables: $\aleph_0$), this entry adds the *next aleph* to the tower: $\mathbb{Q} = \text{Comp} = \text{Alg} = \aleph_0$ (this entry + computables) $\;<\;$ $\omega_1 = \aleph_1$ (companion entry) $\;\leq\;$ $\mathfrak{c} = 2^{\aleph_0}$ (transcendentals entry), with the $\aleph_1 \leq \mathfrak{c}$ inequality independent of ZFC. The four cross-references together exhibit the entire CH question in a single diagram with concrete Lean-formalized representatives at each cardinal level.

**P-adic Liouville theorem: parallel construction of explicit transcendentals in the non-archimedean setting.** This entry's existing `liouville-theorem` cross-reference covers the *archimedean* construction (Liouville 1844 — explicit reals like $\sum 10^{-n!}$ that are too-well-approximated by rationals to be algebraic); `liouville-theorem-oq-04` extends the same approximation-theoretic strategy to the *p-adic* setting, proving that p-adic algebraic numbers cannot be p-adically Liouville (well-approximated by p-adic rationals beyond the degree bound). **Why this matters for the present file**: the present file proves $|\text{Alg}(\mathbb{C})| = \aleph_0$ over the *complex* base field, but the same combinatorial machinery — enumerate $\mathbb{Q}[X]$ as a countable union and take the union over the (finite) roots of each polynomial — applies verbatim to $\overline{\mathbb{Q}_p}$, the algebraic closure of the p-adic field, yielding $|\text{Alg}(\mathbb{Q}_p)| = \aleph_0$ uniformly across all completions of $\mathbb{Q}$. The companion entry's p-adic Liouville theorem then provides the *transcendental* witness in the p-adic complement: p-adically Liouville numbers exist (the p-adic analogue of $\sum 10^{-n!}$) and are p-adically transcendental, proving $\mathbb{Q}_p \setminus \text{Alg}(\mathbb{Q}_p) \neq \emptyset$ — the p-adic version of this entry's archimedean transcendence corollary (`exists_transcendental_real`). **Archimedean ↔ non-archimedean duality**: the four-place cross-reference matrix is now {archimedean countability (this entry), archimedean transcendence witness (`liouville-theorem`), non-archimedean countability (implicit in the same proof generalized), non-archimedean transcendence witness (`liouville-theorem-oq-04`)} — exhibiting the *uniformity* of the algebraic-vs-transcendental cardinality split across all completions of $\mathbb{Q}$ (Ostrowski 1916: every absolute value on $\mathbb{Q}$ is either archimedean or equivalent to a p-adic absolute value).

references.note: Original proof that algebraic numbers are countable; the same paper contains the first uncountability proof of the reals via the nested-intervals argument

references.title: Sur la fonction exponentielle
references.venue: Comptes rendus de l'Académie des Sciences
references.note: First proof that e is transcendental; the method was extended by Lindemann (1882) to prove π transcendental and generalized to the Lindemann-Weierstrass theorem

references.title: Sur des classes très étendues de quantités dont la valeur n'est ni algébrique, ni même réductible à des irrationnelles algébriques
references.venue: Journal de Mathématiques Pures et Appliquées
references.note: First constructive existence proof of transcendental numbers via Diophantine approximation bounds; complements Cantor's cardinality argument by giving explicit examples

references.title: Über die Zahl π
references.note: Proves π is transcendental using Hermite's exponential method; together with Cantor's countability result, establishes that specific transcendentals are hard to identify despite 'almost all' reals being transcendental. Lindemann's argument generalized Hermite's 1873 transcendence proof of $e$ by applying it to $e^{i\pi} = -1$ — a non-trivial algebraic relation that would contradict transcendence of $i\pi$. The paper closes 2200 years of squaring-the-circle attempts (Anaxagoras c. 450 BCE through Lindemann 1882). Cited in keyInsight #13.

references.title: Zu Lindemann's Abhandlung: 'Über die Ludolph'sche Zahl'
references.venue: Sitzungsberichte der Königlich Preussischen Akademie der Wissenschaften zu Berlin 5: 1067–1085
references.note: Weierstrass's generalization of Lindemann's 1882 $\pi$-transcendence proof to the **Lindemann-Weierstrass theorem**: for distinct algebraic numbers $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n \in \overline{\mathbb{Q}}$, the exponentials $e^{\alpha_1}, \ldots, e^{\alpha_n}$ are linearly independent over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$. This is the canonical bridge from algebraic numbers to specific transcendentals, producing infinitely many explicit transcendentals like $e^{\sqrt{2}}, e^{2^{1/3}}, e^{(1+\sqrt{5})/2}$ as exponentials of non-zero algebraic numbers. The proof uses symmetric polynomial bookkeeping over the Galois closure of $\{\alpha_i\}$ combined with Hermite's integral identities for $\int_0^a e^x f(x)\,dx$. Lindemann's $\pi$-transcendence is the $n=2$ case with $(\alpha_1, \alpha_2) = (i\pi, 0)$; Hermite's $e$-transcendence is the $n=1$ case. Cited in keyInsight #13.

references.title: Sur le septième Problème de Hilbert
references.note: Gelfond's 1934 proof (independent from Schneider's same-year proof) of **Hilbert's 7th problem**: if $\alpha \in \overline{\mathbb{Q}} \setminus \{0, 1\}$ and $\beta \in \overline{\mathbb{Q}} \setminus \mathbb{Q}$, then $\alpha^\beta$ is transcendental. Concretely establishes the transcendence of Gelfond's constant $e^\pi = (-1)^{-i}$, the Gelfond-Schneider constant $2^{\sqrt{2}}$, and $\log_b a$ for algebraic $a, b > 0$ with $a \neq 1$ and $\log_b a$ irrational. The proof uses analytic estimates on $a^z$ as an entire function of $z$, with delicate $p$-adic refinements distinct from Lindemann-Weierstrass's symmetric-polynomial method. Combined with Lindemann-Weierstrass, this gives the **two great transcendence theorems of pre-1960 transcendence theory**, both subsumed (conjecturally) by Schanuel's conjecture (1960s). Cited in keyInsight #13.

references.title: Irrational Numbers
references.venue: Carus Mathematical Monographs No. 11, Mathematical Association of America
references.note: The standard introductory reference on algebraic and transcendental number theory. Chapter 5 develops the countability of algebraic numbers via the height-function approach, complementing the abstract Mathlib-based proof formalized here. Provides accessible elementary proofs of e and π transcendence, the Lindemann-Weierstrass theorem, and the Gelfond-Schneider theorem.

references.title: Making Transcendence Transparent: An Intuitive Approach to Classical Transcendental Number Theory
references.note: Modern accessible treatment of transcendence theory connecting Cantor's countability argument (Chapter 1) to Liouville's construction (Chapter 2), Hermite-Lindemann (Chapter 3), Gelfond-Schneider (Chapter 4), and Baker's theorem (Chapter 5). Particularly valuable for understanding the dialectic between cardinality-based and construction-based approaches to identifying transcendental numbers — the very contrast highlighted in this entry's openQuestions and cross-references to liouville-theorem and hermite-lindemann.

references.title: Was sind und was sollen die Zahlen?
references.note: Dedekind's foundational treatise on set theory and the natural numbers, published 14 years after Cantor's 1874 result. Introduces the formal definition of an infinite set as one equinumerous with a proper subset — the precise property exhibited here as $|\text{algebraic reals}| = |\mathbb{Q}|$ despite $\mathbb{Q} \subsetneq \text{algebraic reals}$. This is the conceptual underpinning of the 'cardinal paradox' formalized in `card_algebraic_eq_card_rat`.

references.title: Topics in Galois Theory
references.note: Standard modern reference for the absolute Galois group $\text{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})$ and its action on algebraic numbers; treats orbit decomposition by minimal polynomial and connects to the inverse Galois problem

references.title: Transcendental Number Theory
references.note: Comprehensive monograph on transcendence; chapter 1 reviews Cantor's countability argument and Liouville's construction; later chapters cover Baker's theorem on linear forms in logarithms (Fields Medal 1970), the most powerful effective transcendence tool

references.title: Lectures on Transcendental Numbers
references.note: Mahler's lecture notes synthesize the classical transcendence results from his own work in the 1930s onwards. Chapter 1 reviews Cantor's countability argument and the dichotomy between cardinal-existence and explicit-construction proofs; subsequent chapters develop the Mahler classification of transcendental numbers ($A$, $S$, $T$, $U$ types) which is a finer-grained partition of the uncountable transcendental complement first established by Cantor's countability argument formalized here. The Mahler classification is the natural sequel to 'algebraic numbers are countable' — it asks not 'how many transcendentals are there?' but 'how are they distributed by approximability?'

references.title: An inequality in the theory of arithmetic on algebraic varieties
references.venue: Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society 45, 502–509
references.note: Establishes the Northcott property: for any bounds $(d, B)$, the set of algebraic numbers of degree $\leq d$ and absolute height $\leq B$ is finite. This is the quantitative refinement of Cantor's 1874 countability formalized in this entry — Cantor showed each height-stratum is finite (hence the algebraic numbers are a countable union of finite sets), and Northcott reformulates this with the modern Weil/Mahler absolute height to give effective finiteness bounds. The Northcott property is the foundational counting principle for effective Diophantine geometry, used in Bogomolov's conjecture (Ullmo–Zhang 1998), the Manin–Mumford conjecture, and the equidistribution theorems of Bilu and Bombieri–Zannier.

references.title: Heights in Diophantine Geometry
references.venue: Cambridge University Press, New Mathematical Monographs 4
references.note: Comprehensive modern reference on the theory of heights, the Northcott property, and applications to Diophantine geometry. Chapter 1 reviews the absolute (Weil/Mahler) height and proves the Northcott property in the form referenced in this entry's keyInsight on bounded-height-and-degree finiteness. Connects the elementary countability formalized here to the quantitative finiteness theorems that power Faltings' theorem, the Mordell–Lang conjecture, and effective transcendence bounds.

references.title: Sur le septième Problème de Hilbert
references.venue: Doklady Akademii Nauk SSSR 2: 1–6 (full version: Izvestiya Akademii Nauk SSSR, Seriya Matematicheskaya 7: 623–634, 1934)
references.note: Gel'fond's independent proof — simultaneous with Schneider — of **Hilbert's 7th problem**: if $\alpha$ is algebraic with $\alpha \neq 0, 1$ and $\beta$ is irrational algebraic, then $\alpha^\beta$ is transcendental. In particular $2^{\sqrt{2}}$ and $e^\pi = (-1)^{-i}$ are transcendental, the latter being the *Gel'fond constant*. Gel'fond's method introduces interpolation determinants and algebraic-integer arithmetic in $\mathbb{Z}[i]$, the technical seed of what becomes Baker's method (1966, addressed in companion entry `algebraic-numbers-countable-oq-04`). For this entry's countability framework, Gel'fond-Schneider sharpens the abstract uncountability of transcendentals (keyInsight #3) to *individual* transcendence verifications of explicit numbers — exhibiting concrete elements of the $2^{\aleph_0}$-cardinality transcendental complement. Cited in openQuestion #2 (companion entry `gelfond-schneider`) and keyInsight #9 (Mahler's classification refinement).

references.title: Transzendenzuntersuchungen periodischer Funktionen I, II
references.venue: Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik 172: 65–69 (Part I); 70–74 (Part II)
references.note: Schneider's two 1934 papers, independent of Gel'fond's parallel work, give the second proof of **Hilbert's 7th problem** ($\alpha^\beta$ transcendental for $\alpha$ algebraic $\neq 0, 1$ and $\beta$ irrational algebraic). Schneider's method is more general than Gel'fond's, using analytic auxiliary functions vanishing to high order at many algebraic points, and extends naturally to transcendence statements about elliptic functions, modular functions, and abelian integrals. Schneider 1937 proves transcendence of $j(\tau)$ for $\tau$ algebraic of positive imaginary part, the foundation of the modern transcendence theory of periods. Cited in openQuestion #2 alongside Gel'fond 1934; together they form the **Gel'fond-Schneider theorem**, settling one of the four explicitly-listed Hilbert problems concerning transcendence.

references.title: Linear forms in the logarithms of algebraic numbers I, II, III, IV
references.note: Baker's quartet of 1966 papers proving the **Baker theorem on linear forms in logarithms**: if $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n$ are non-zero algebraic numbers and $\log \alpha_1, \ldots, \log \alpha_n$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$, then they are linearly independent over the algebraic closure $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$. Baker won the 1970 Fields Medal for this work. The theorem dramatically generalizes Gel'fond-Schneider: setting $n = 2$ and rearranging gives $\alpha^\beta = \exp(\beta \log \alpha)$ transcendental. Baker's deeper innovation is **effective transcendence**: the theorem comes with explicit lower bounds $|b_1 \log \alpha_1 + \cdots + b_n \log \alpha_n| > C / B^\kappa$ for $b_i \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $\max |b_i| \leq B$, yielding effective solutions to Diophantine equations (Mordell's conjecture for elliptic curves, Catalan's conjecture in special cases). Cited in openQuestion #3 (companion entry `algebraic-numbers-countable-oq-04` formalizes Baker's theorem).

references.title: Rational approximations to algebraic numbers
references.note: Roth's theorem: for any algebraic number $\alpha$ of degree $\geq 2$ and any $\epsilon > 0$, the inequality $|\alpha - p/q| < q^{-(2 + \epsilon)}$ has only finitely many rational solutions $p/q$. This is the **best possible exponent** (since Dirichlet's theorem gives infinitely many with exponent 2), settling a chain of refinements from Liouville (1844, exponent equal to the degree $n$), through Thue (1909, exponent $n/2 + 1$), Siegel (1921, exponent $2\sqrt{n}$), Dyson and Gel'fond (1947–1948, exponent $\sqrt{2n}$) to Roth's optimal $2 + \epsilon$. Roth won the 1958 Fields Medal. The theorem is non-effective: it proves *finitely* many solutions but cannot bound them. Connects to this entry's keyInsight #5 on the **Liouville-Cantor complementarity**: Liouville's 1844 construction exploits a wider Diophantine gap than algebraic numbers can achieve; Roth's theorem makes this gap precise (algebraic numbers admit *no* such super-quadratic approximations). Foundational for modern Diophantine geometry.

references.title: Irrationalité de $\zeta(2)$ et $\zeta(3)$
references.note: Apéry's celebrated 1979 announcement (with full proofs surfaced in van der Poorten's explanatory paper *A proof that Euler missed*, Mathematical Intelligencer 1: 195–203, 1979) that $\zeta(3) = \sum_{n \geq 1} 1/n^3$ is **irrational** — the first non-trivial irrationality result for the values $\zeta(2k+1)$ of the Riemann zeta function at odd integers. Apéry's proof uses fast-converging series $\zeta(3) = \frac{5}{2} \sum_{n=1}^\infty (-1)^{n-1}/(n^3 \binom{2n}{n})$ and a Diophantine approximation argument requiring no advanced apparatus. Despite 47 years of intensive work, the irrationality of $\zeta(5), \zeta(7), \zeta(9), \zeta(11)$ remains open — only Rivoal-Ball (2001) showed infinitely many odd $\zeta(2k+1)$ are irrational, and Zudilin (2001) sharpened to 'at least one of $\zeta(5), \zeta(7), \zeta(9), \zeta(11)$ is irrational'. Concrete instance of the abstract transcendental/irrational complement this entry's countability argument identifies: $\zeta(3) \in \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}$, and whether $\zeta(3) \in \overline{\mathbb{Q}}^c$ (transcendence) remains a major open question.
